         Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA TSC”) (together, “Applicants”) hereby respectfully submit these exceptions

to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) issued by the State Office of Administrative Hearings

(“SOAH”) Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) on August 20, 2026, regarding the Bell County

East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765 kV transmission line project (“Project”) with respect to

processing, notice, and routing 1 and consolidated with the Big Hill Substation to Sand Lake Switch

765 kV transmission line project (collectively with the Project, the “Import Path 2 Projects”) with

respect to need. The Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) established September

2, 2026, as the deadline for parties to file exceptions to the PFD. 2 Therefore, these exceptions are

timely filed.

                                          I.    INTRODUCTION

witness testimony regarding complex grid infrastructure and power flow dynamics, among many

       Applicants urge the Commission to reject the PFD’s incorrect recommendations and issue

               II.   EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

       Applicants recognize the voluminous record and the ALJs’ attempt to consider the complex

issues raised in this critical proceeding for the reliability of the Permian Basin region and the

overall interconnected ERCOT grid. Respectfully, however, the ALJs erred in applying the

Commission’s rules and Commission precedent to the record in this docket.           Accordingly,

Applicants submit the following exceptions and corrections to the PFD’s proposed findings of fact,

conclusions of law, and ordering paragraphs.

A. Executive Summary

       Applicants’ Exceptions to the PFD focus primarily on the findings that were determinative

in the ALJs’ recommendation of denial, namely that Applicants failed to establish the need for the

Import Path 2 Projects and failed to comply with the Commission’s rules concerning public

participation meetings and notice of the Project Application. The errors in the PFD’s findings and

conclusions are discussed in detail below, with this section serving as an executive summary of

the Applicants’ key points of disagreement with the PFD.

       The PFD’s most consequential error is its recommendation that Applicants failed to

establish that the Import Path 2 Projects are necessary under PURA § 37.056. That conclusion is

wrong for multiple independent reasons. The Import Path 2 Projects are not an untested solution

to a hypothetical problem that is unlikely to materialize. They are, rather, an indispensable

component of a legislatively directed, Commission-approved, ERCOT-planned transmission

solution for the Permian Basin region. The PFD’s contrary conclusion disregards the legal and

technical framework governing transmission planning and substitutes speculation for the reasoned

determinations of the Commission and ERCOT.




APPLICANTS’ EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                                    Page 6 of 80
         First, the Commission and six presiding officers across three other dockets have already

found that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) alone is sufficient to establish the need

for the recommended 765 kV transmission infrastructure. 5 The Commission granted CCNs for

both projects comprising Import Path 1, finding in each case that the PBRP establishes the need

for additional service in the Permian Basin. That finding applies with equal force to the Import

Path 2 Projects, which are an integrated component of the same reliability plan. Likewise, the

ALJs presiding over the docket concerning Import Path 3 recommended finding the need was

established. 6    The PFD’s contrary conclusion is an outlier that conflicts with these prior

determinations and the Commission’s established approach to approving components of

coordinated ERCOT transmission plans.

        Second, the PFD concluded that ERCOT’s recommendation provided in the PBRP is not

entitled to “great weight” under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II). That conclusion directly

contradicts the plain language of the Commission’s rule, which provides that the Commission “will

give great weight” to ERCOT’s recommendation for a reliability project. This rule is not

discretionary. The PFD reasons that ERCOT’s later adoption of a different load-forecasting

methodology for the 2025 Regional Transmission Plan (“RTP”) somehow rendered the PBRP

recommendation invalid. But ERCOT itself continues to recommend the Import Path 2 Projects

notwithstanding that methodology change, as reflected in the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP, and the

Critically, the 2025 RTP applied the updated methodology and still included the 765 kV import

paths in its base assumptions. The later methodology did not withdraw, amend, or supersede the

PBRP.

        Third, no party challenging the need independently analyzed the Import Path 2 Projects’

need through power-flow studies, steady-state analyses, or other accepted system planning

assessments that could even purport to rebut ERCOT’s work. No party modeled a reliable

alternative with the Import Path 2 Projects removed. The PFD’s need determination therefore rests

on non-expert opinions, not competing technical analysis. Those opinions lack the engineering

rigor required to overcome the great weight owed to ERCOT’s recommendation, particularly

where ERCOT’s studies evaluated contingencies, load, generation, and transmission topology

under North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) Reliability Standards and in

accordance with the ERCOT Planning Guide. The PFD cannot replace sophisticated and highly

technical reliability analysis with unverified and unsupported conjecture and bald declarations.

        Fourth, the Far West Texas Import GTCs independently demonstrate that the Import Path

2 Projects are needed today, regardless of whether additional load materializes. The GTCs reflect

the physical limits of the existing 345-kV transmission infrastructure and an imminent threat of

firm load shed in Far West Texas exceeding 2,000 MW. ERCOT’s April 2026 GTC exit strategy

identifies all three 765-kV import paths—including the Import Path 2 Projects—as essential to

retiring the GTCs by 2030, even assuming that approximately 2,500 MW of planned dispatchable

generation materializes. The GTCs provide a present-day, reliability-based need for the Import

Path 2 Projects that does not depend on the PBRP’s forecast of future load. This basis alone

compels approval of the Import Path 2 Projects.



APPLICANTS’ EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                                    Page 8 of 80
         Fifth, the PFD supports its conclusions with lay testimony suggesting that expected

generation in the Permian Basin is sufficient to obviate the need to import additional power. The

full record does not support that premise. The 39 GW of announced generation cited in the PFD

consists almost entirely of projects that are not under construction; only 1.35 GW of capacity were

under construction as of May 2026. Some identified generators would not even be interconnected

with ERCOT, so they cannot contribute to ERCOT grid reliability. Announcements therefore do

not establish timely, deliverable capacity or an equivalent alternative to system transmission

facilities. ERCOT’s planning analyses already accounted for planned generation, and its GTC exit

strategy retained all three 765-kV paths even while assuming additional dispatchable generation

in the future.

        Simply put, there is no credible evidence in the record that can override the four separate

ERCOT studies that are entitled to “great weight” under the law and each independently found

that the Import Path 2 Projects are imminently needed for the reliability of the ERCOT system.

There is no better evidence that a project is needed for reliability than an undisputed finding from

the independent grid operator that load shed will be required to address system conditions that

exist today.

        The PFD’s notice-related grounds for denial are likewise unsupported. On the public-

meeting issue, 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) requires at least one pre-application public meeting, direct-

mail notice to landowners within 500 feet of the preliminary route centerline, and written notice

to the Department of Defense; it does not require a new meeting whenever routes links are added

or modified. That plain-language reading is confirmed by decades of Commission precedent and

was most recently confirmed by the Commission just last week in Docket No. 59315. The PFD’s

 novel “scale and complexity” standard finds no support in the rule’s text, Commission precedent,

       With respect to the issue regarding notice of the Project Application, the PFD’s

interpretation of “current county tax rolls” is also unsupported by the rule’s text or Commission

precedent. The Commission recently declined to revise the notice rule to require a specific date

for verification of landowner ownership through county-tax-roll data, finding the existing process

Commission’s notice rule also renders the rule’s notice-cure provision a nullity by treating any

expressly contemplates cure for newly identified landowners entitled to notice.

       Moreover, denial would not be a permissible remedy for the alleged notice issues. Even if
